THE TEXT Original short fiction

A story about making room

The unpainted square

By the time the others arrived, Amira had already decided where everything belonged.

01Amira spread her drawing across the folding table. On paper, the wall outside the community centre was already finished: blue buildings, yellow windows, a river that curved neatly around them. She had measured every section twice. Beside the drawing, six paintbrushes lay in a straight line, their handles pointing towards her.

02When the volunteers arrived, she handed each one a numbered section. Mr Chen studied his for a moment. “Where is the old bakery?” he asked. Amira explained that the bakery had closed years ago. “I know,” he said. “But that is where I met my wife.” He folded the paper carefully and waited.

03Soon everyone had a place to add: the bus stop where a friendship began, a tree that had survived a storm, the shop with a cat in its window. Amira looked from their hands to her drawing. Every new story needed space she had already filled. She pressed her ruler against the edge of the paper.

04Her little brother put an empty jam jar on the table. “For mixing colours,” he said. Its glass was cloudy, and the label was still half attached. Amira almost told him to fetch a clean one. Instead, she dropped a little blue and yellow into it and watched a green appear that was nowhere in her plan.

05She turned the drawing over. On the blank side, she sketched the river again, this time leaving its banks open. Then she pushed the brushes into the middle of the table. “Show me where the bakery was,” she said. When they began painting, she left one square of the wall untouched. She did not yet know whose story would go there.

End of passage ✦

From the references to your app

Patterns & proposed UI

What we learned from the lesson screens, and what that means for your Grade 9 app.

What the research actually changes

Five findings from the inspected lessons. Click either image to inspect the exact screen. Proposed decisions are our interpretation—not measured learning outcomes.

01 Fishtank changes the materials more than the grade UI

Grade 7 · embedded article · live preview ↗ Grade 9 · external resource · live preview ↗

Observed: Across one sampled task per grade, Grades 3–12 reused the response editor. Grade 7 embedded its article; Grade 9 linked to Identity Charts; Grade 12 embedded video.

For our app: Use one lesson workspace with different material types. These samples give us no reason to create a separate interface for each grade.

02 Questions can interrupt reading—or stay beside it

Actively Learn · embedded questions · teacher preview ↗ Quill · passage + task · live lesson ↗

Observed: Actively Learn places questions within the article. Quill keeps the passage beside a focused response task. These are different ways of pacing the lesson.

For our app: For sustained Grade 9 analysis, start with a persistent passage and a task panel. Use in-text checkpoints deliberately when a lesson needs a pause; test the trade-off with students.

03 Short evidence practice and essay writing need different editors

Quill · short response + feedback · live lesson ↗ Soar/Summit · paragraph fields · publisher demo, Grade 7 context ↗

Observed: Quill used the same sentence stem with because, but and so to elicit a cause, a contrast and a consequence—three reasoning moves, not simply three text boxes. The publisher writing demo broke a longer response into introduction and body-paragraph fields, with prompt and criteria alongside.

For our app: Prototype sentence stems tied to a named reasoning move, rather than a generic blank answer box. Add a structured long-writing mode only for lessons that teach extended composition. The Soar comparison is a demo, not verified Grade 9 access.

04Verified: Quill responds to missing reasoning, then accepts a revision

Attempt 1 · weak explanation · live recheck ↗Attempt 2 · revised explanation accepted · live recheck ↗

Observed: I completed the because stem with “coral reefs are important to the ocean.” Quill asked why sound reveals reef health and explained the function of because. It accepted a revision contrasting noisy healthy reefs with quieter damaged reefs. The unchanged answer could not be resubmitted.

Design hypothesis: Give a hint about the missing reasoning before revealing a model answer, keeping the response editable. This test confirms one successful feedback → revision path; it does not establish diagnostic accuracy across students or answer types.

05 An assignment screen does not supply the teaching by itself

Fishtank · assigned task · live student preview ↗ Oak · teacher explanation · live lesson ↗

Observed: The Fishtank Grade 9 preview exposed a resource and response task within a teacher-assigned curriculum. Oak’s inspected lesson supplied teacher video, a starter quiz and an exit quiz. Seneca instead taught through short explanation cards.

For our app: If students will use the app independently, prototype a worked example before the first evidence task. A passage and answer box alone do not show students how to analyse. This is our proposal, not an effectiveness finding.

2 She unfolded the invitation, then folded it again before anyone could see her name.

3 When the door opened, she said she was only looking for the library.

Selected evidence · paragraph 2
B · One focused task

What suggests that Maya wants to join but is hesitant?

C · Connect evidence to reasoning
“She unfolded the invitation, then folded it again…” Paragraph 2 · linked to the passage
Maya seems interested because she keeps the invitation, but hiding her name suggests she is afraid to be noticed.

You identified hesitation. Explain how her excuse about the library supports your interpretation.

Usability basics · clear actions, readable text, autosave & accessibility

Baseline requirements for the whole app. Kept separate from the reading-specific design ideas.

Give one clear next action

Show the lesson goal, current step and one primary action: read, respond, check or revise.

Make reading comfortable

Start with adjustable 18–20px passage text and generous spacing. Test these design choices with students.

Protect the student’s work

Autosave drafts, show save status and resume at the last step. Keep “Save” and “Submit” visibly distinct.

Build access into every screen

Support keyboard use, visible focus, zoom and labeled controls. Meet text contrast requirements; aim for 44px controls.

Curriculum rationale & validation checks

Curriculum: CCSS RL.9–10.1 calls for evidence-backed literary analysis; W.9–10.9 connects evidence from reading to writing. This supports the evidence → explanation → revision flow. Standards specify learning expectations, not a required screen layout. Map individual lessons separately to your chosen state curriculum.

CCSS reading, Grades 9–10 ↗CCSS writing, Grades 9–10 ↗

Accessibility: use WCAG 2.2 AA as a baseline: keyboard operation, visible focus, normal-text contrast of at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for qualifying large text), and text resizing to 200%. WCAG’s minimum target-size criterion is 24×24 CSS pixels with exceptions; the 44px control target in Usability basics is our more generous design recommendation. These are selected checks, not a complete conformance audit.

WCAG 2.2 ↗Target-size details ↗

Before shipping: ask students to resume a lesson, find evidence, explain an answer and revise it without adult guidance. Check the same tasks on a small screen and with keyboard-only input. Shared UI patterns alone do not prove better learning outcomes.

What this library includes

The main view contains teaching, reading, questions, writing and feedback screens. Course menus, marketing pages and printable PDFs are excluded from the image galleries.

Evidence labels: “Live lesson” means the lesson was opened and explored. “Preview” means a restricted or teacher-preview view. “Publisher walkthrough” means screenshots shown in an official demo. “Web study notes” and “Classroom task guide” are not interactive student assignments.

Exact completion and curriculum checks are in each app’s notes. UK GCSE/IGCSE examples are roughly ages 14–16; they do not establish US Grade 11–12 coverage.
